findings.title: definite nominal praise stands before the genitive chain
findings.claim: The ayah presents praise as an established topic and then assigns it through the following governed phrase, rather than narrating a speaker's timed act of praising.
findings.mechanism: The definite nominal form al-hamdu occupies the opening topic position; the following li-Allāh phrase functions as its predicate, so the clause is built as a stable assertion before the genitive chain widens it.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader hears the opening as a settled declaration of praise, not merely as the compressed Turkish word 'övgü'.
findings.containment: The ordinary 'Her türlü övgü Allah'a, bütün varlıkların Rabbine aittir' floor remains intact; the supplied contrastive variants are not treated as alternate local parses.

epistemic.reason: Local syntax and the accepted QAC-aligned word analysis directly support the nominal-topic and predicate relation.

findings.title: the opening stance moves from invocation to praise
findings.claim: The first full declaration turns the basmala's invocation of Allah into a stance of praise that opens the ayah.
findings.mechanism: The first-word placement, nominative ending, suppressed speaker, and supplied 1:1 boundary evidence move the discourse from naming or invoking to presenting praise.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader perceives why the ayah begins with a posture before causes, requests, or human agency appear.
findings.containment: This is a local opening and boundary effect around the same primary praise claim, not a replacement of the invocation or a surah-wide thesis.

epistemic.reason: The focus word position, form, and supplied boundary evidence jointly support the discourse movement.

findings.title: praise joins a recurring deity-lordship-worlds cluster
findings.claim: The opening praise is framed as the first member of the supplied praise-to-Allah-lordship-worlds formula.
findings.mechanism: The definite praise topic is immediately linked to Allah, Rabb, and alamin in the same clause, and the supplied collocation evidence identifies the recurring formulaic shape.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the first word already points toward a praise relation that the rest of the ayah expands through name, title, and scope.
findings.containment: This records a supplied local and formulaic linkage; it does not claim a surah-wide architecture or make the formula replace the plain attribution.

epistemic.reason: The named relations are all present in the focus clause and are supported by the accepted word-analysis records.

findings.title: praise includes recognition, gratitude, and commendation

findings.mechanism: The focus noun's supplied semantic range places evaluative recognition and thanks within the same lexical field, while the nominal form keeps the local declaration as the general act of praise.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader sees why a translation's 'övgü' can still carry gratitude and recognition without becoming only 'teşekkür'.
findings.containment: The finding keeps the local noun's bounded praise range and does not activate remote idiomatic forms or turn the noun into a finite speaker action.

epistemic.reason: The accepted focus analysis explicitly supplies the range and its local boundary.

findings.reader_payoff: The reader can hear the small particle as part of the praise assignment rather than as a detachable translation word.
findings.containment: Sound reinforces the dependency; it adds no new referent or independent semantic branch.

epistemic.reason: The supplied surface and accepted syntax directly support both binding and governance.

findings.reader_payoff: The reader notices a precise grammatical change: the name once invoked is now the named holder and recipient of praise.
findings.containment: The referent remains Allah; only the clause's relation to the name changes.
